steps.prompt: Why does every modern AI run on 'attention'?
steps.sub: To understand a word, a model must look at the RIGHT other words. That's attention — and the transformer is just attention stacked into a tower. By the end you'll know what attention does, what a transformer block holds, and why it beat everything before it.

steps.prompt: In 'The animal didn't cross the street because IT was too tired' — what does a model need to figure out 'it'?

options.t: Just read the words left to right and hope.
Look back at the other words and decide 'it' refers to 'animal', not 'street'.
Count the letters in the sentence.

steps.why: Understanding 'it' means looking at the right earlier word and weighting it heavily — 'animal' matters here, 'street' doesn't. That selective looking-at-the-right-words IS attention. Reading blindly or counting letters can't resolve the reference.
hints: Which earlier word does 'it' point to — and how would the model know?
It has to focus on 'animal' more than 'street'. What's that focusing called?

steps.sub: Tap each card. This is the heart of it.

cards.b: Every token sends out a 'query': which other words should I pay attention to right now?
Every token also has a 'key' (what it offers). Query meets keys → a relevance score for each other word.
The word pulls in a weighted mix of the others' 'values' — more from relevant words, less from irrelevant ones. Now each word's meaning is shaped by context.

steps.prompt: In one line, what does attention let a model do?

options.t: Weigh which other tokens matter for understanding each token.
Make the model run on a GPU.
Compress the text to save memory.

steps.why: Attention is a weighting mechanism: for each word, it decides how much every other word should count toward that word's meaning. It's not about hardware or compression — it's about context, letting each token 'see' the relevant rest of the sentence.
hints: It's about deciding what to FOCUS on, per word.
Weighing which other tokens matter — that's the one-liner.

steps.prompt: Why attention beat what came before (RNNs).
steps.sub: Tap each card — this is why transformers won.

cards.h: Old way: one word at a time
cards.b: RNNs read left-to-right, sequentially. Long sentences = long chains, and early words fade by the end.
Attention looks at ALL words in parallel — no waiting in line. Perfect for GPUs, so training scales massively.
Word 1 can attend directly to word 100 with no fading. Long-range links stay strong.

steps.prompt: Old RNN way vs new attention way — sort each trait.
steps.sub: Tap a trait, then its bin.

items.t: Processes words one at a time, in sequence
Early words fade over long sentences
Word 1 can link directly to word 100, no fading
Hard to use a GPU's full power

hints: Sequential + fading + GPU-unfriendly = the old way.
Parallel + long-range links that stay strong = attention.

steps.sub: Tap each card — stack this block N times and you get an LLM.

cards.b: Each token mixes in context from the other tokens — the part you just learned.
A small per-token neural net that further processes each token's now-contextual vector.
Repeat the block many times (12, 96, …). Each layer builds richer understanding. That tower IS the transformer.

steps.prompt: Trace one token through a transformer block, in order.
steps.sub: Tap the steps in the order they happen.
chips: Feed-forward layer processes each token further
Token enters as a vector (its embedding)
Attention mixes in context from other tokens
Pass the result up to the next block
hints: It starts as an embedding before any mixing happens.
Embedding in → attention (context) → feed-forward → up to next block.

steps.sub: Sentence: 'The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big.' Pick the next move each turn.
steps.goal: Use attention to figure out what 'it' refers to.

turns.situation: The model reaches the word 'it' and must understand what it refers to.
turns.q: What does the attention mechanism do first?
options: Send a query from 'it' to score every other word's relevance
Ignore the rest of the sentence
turns.log: 🙋 'it' queries the sentence for relevant words

turns.situation: Scores come back. 'Too big' suggests the thing that was too LARGE to fit.
turns.q: Which word should get the highest attention weight?
options: 'trophy' — the thing that was too big

turns.situation: Attention blends in mostly 'trophy'. The word 'it' is now understood in context.
turns.q: What has the model effectively decided?

hints: 'Too big' is the clue — which object couldn't fit because of its size?
Attention puts the most weight on the most relevant word, then blends it in.

statements.t: Attention lets each token weigh how much every other token matters to it.
statements.why: Yes — that per-token weighting of all the others is exactly what attention computes.

statements.t: Transformers must read words strictly one at a time, like older RNNs.
statements.why: No — they process all tokens in parallel. That parallelism is a big reason they scale and win.

statements.t: A transformer is built from stacked attention + feed-forward blocks.
statements.why: Right — that repeated block, many layers deep, is the whole architecture behind modern LLMs.

statements.t: Attention can directly link a word to a far-away word with no fading.
statements.why: Yes — unlike RNNs, distance doesn't weaken the link; word 1 can attend straight to word 100.

hints: Recall what you sorted: which way is parallel, which is one-at-a-time?
Two statements are true about attention's strengths; one wrongly makes it sequential.

fields.ph: e.g. chatbot for support, summarising docs, code help

fields.label: In your own words, why does 'looking at the right other words' matter for that use?
fields.ph: e.g. it has to track which ticket detail the question refers to

steps.prompt: Final check: why do transformers underlie nearly all modern AI?

options.t: They use less electricity than any other model.
Attention gives rich context AND runs in parallel, so they scale to huge data and sizes.

steps.why: The winning combo: attention captures context (including long-range), and it's parallel, so it rides GPUs to enormous scale. That scalability — not low power or perfection — is why transformers power today's LLMs, vision, and more.
hints: Two reasons together: good at context, AND fast to scale.
Think parallelism + long-range context, not power or perfection.
